transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine will stop attacking Russian oil refineries
if Moscow suspends strikes on Ukrainian energy sites.
NPR's Joanna Gekisys reports Zelensky was responding to President Trump's claim that
he had secured an energy truce between the two countries.
The Kremlin has not commented on the energy truce, and Zelensky says he has not been informed
about it.
In an evening video address on Sunday, he said Ukraine has proposed ways to de-escalate
the war, but Putin has only said one thing, yet or no.
Russia has continued to attack Ukraine since Trump announced the truce.
Russia blames Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising fuel prices.
The strikes are Ukraine's attempt to weaken Russia's war machine.
Energy experts and even Russian authorities have said the U.S. war on Iran is primarily
driving the price hikes.
Joanna Gekisys, NPR News, Kyiv.
Houthi rebels have attacked the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital for the second straight
day.
In NPR's Eija Betrawi reports one person was killed and 11 others were wounded.
Saudi authorities say the deadliest attack in years took place Saturday when a passenger
terminal in the capital, Riyadh, was hit, killing at least 13 people and wounding more
than 300 others.
The attacks have suspended operations at Riyadh Airport and forced oil executives from major
companies to cancel their attendance at an energy summit in the capital this week.
The Houthis say they're attacking Saudi airport's Aniramco energy sites with missiles and drones
in response to Saudi airstrikes on Yemen that have killed civilians there too.
The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, are also blocking Saudi oil tankers from using the
Red Sea shipping strait.
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Iran held a call on Sunday to discuss the
recent escalation.
Aya Bultrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
The Nobel Prize in Economics is being shared by two Americans, Robert Hall of Stanford
University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, study how decisions by households
and businesses shape the economy.
Hall's research examines how spending and hiring impacts recessions and recoveries.
Woodford's work explains how central banks can use interest rates to keep inflation in
check.
Cleanup efforts are continuing across the southeast after Hurricane Esai Iyas, but another weather
threat is emerging.
Forecasters are warning of record-breaking heat along the Gulf Coast this week.
Lauren Lineb, a member station, WVHM reports.
If you're seeing high temperatures get into the upper 80s and low 90s and you're still
without power, people without AC, that's going to be pretty rough when they're still trying
to do cleanup.
So the National Weather Service has been recommending working during the cooler hours of the day.
That's Lauren Lineb reporting from Birmingham, Alabama.
This is NPR News.
Many leaders of Native American tribal nations are raising concerns about the Trump administration's
proposal for unprecedented changes to the next U.S. census.
It would reshape voting maps and how federal funding is distributed across the United States.
NPR's Hansi Lowong reports.
One proposed change is not to use the 2030 census to produce statistics about race and
ethnicity.
The topic has been part of the U.S. headcount since the first one in 1790.
Trump officials say they see a "reduced need" for that information, which is used for redistricting
and enforcing civil rights laws.
Megan Bishop of the National Congress of American Indians is an enrolled citizen of the native
village of Afognac in Alaska.
There's a significant concern about how federal funding would be distributed through grants
and other programs to tribes if that race-ethnicity census question is erased.
The public can comment on their proposal through November 2nd.
Hansi Lowong, NPR News.
A federal judge has ordered the White House to cancel any remaining taxpayer-funded television
ads promoting President Trump's political messages.
The Department of Homeland Security allocated $20 million for the campaign.
The judge issued a two-week restraining order Sunday night in a lawsuit challenging the spending.
The administration had argued the order was unnecessary because the ads were about to
stop airing.
The White House has defended the commercials as public service announcements.
I'm Windsor Johnston, and you're listening to NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: Zelensky says Ukraine will halt refinery strikes if Moscow suspends energy site attacks
Houthi rebels attack Riyadh airport for second straight day, killing one and wounding 11
Nobel Prize in Economics shared by Robert Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia
Cleanup continues across Southeast after Hurricane Helene, with record heat forecast on Gulf Coast
Tribal leaders raise concerns over Trump administration's proposed changes to 2030 census
Federal judge orders White House to cancel remaining taxpayer-funded Trump political TV ads
